body:
Digital infrastructure must remain reliable and accountable

A shared digital system may be used by many government departments, businesses and citizens. If it becomes unreliable, its failure can affect several services at once. The public value of such a system therefore depends not only on its technical capability but also on the quality of its governance, accessibility and maintenance.

Governance means the rules, responsibilities and institutional arrangements through which a system is operated, supervised and held accountable. In digital public infrastructure, governance should establish who can participate, which information may be accessed, who responds to failures and how users can raise complaints.

Important governance requirements

  • Clear institutional responsibility: A defined organisation should be accountable for maintaining a system and applying its governing rules.
  • Privacy and security: Identity and other personal information should be protected through appropriate controls and applicable legal safeguards.
  • Fair participation: Suitable rules should permit eligible organisations to participate without unnecessary discrimination.
  • Transparency: Relevant rules, eligibility conditions and service procedures should be understandable and accessible.
  • Redressal: Users should have appropriate means to report errors, unauthorized activity or wrongful denial of service.
  • Continuity: Services should plan for interruptions, recover from failures and maintain reliable records.

Open-source licensing can permit the inspection or adaptation of software, but it does not automatically guarantee that a deployed service is secure, fair or properly governed. Those outcomes depend on implementation and continuing oversight.

Sustainability has several dimensions

Technical sustainability requires regular maintenance, updates, testing, documentation and the ability to repair or replace components. A system that works when launched may become unreliable if it is not maintained.

Financial sustainability concerns the continuing cost of infrastructure, connectivity, electricity, security, trained personnel and support. Even when software carries no licence fee, operation and maintenance are not costless.

Institutional sustainability requires stable responsibility, trained personnel, compatible procedures and the capacity to improve the system as needs change.

Social sustainability requires that the system remain usable by people with different levels of digital literacy, income, language proficiency and physical ability. A service that works only for people who own smartphones cannot, by that fact alone, ensure universal access.

Environmental sustainability includes using equipment and energy efficiently and managing electronic waste responsibly. Digital services may reduce some paper use and travel, but computers, networks and data centres still consume energy and materials.

Open technology and long-term control

Open standards can reduce dependence on a single supplier by allowing different compatible implementations. Open-source software can support local adaptation and reuse. Appropriate documentation allows new teams to understand and maintain a system.

However, each benefit depends on the actual licence, available skills, quality of documentation and continuing support. A poorly maintained open-source system can be less useful than a well-governed alternative.

Accessibility and alternative service channels

Digital public infrastructure should not be confused with digital-only service delivery. Citizens may need assisted access through local service centres, reliable offline procedures or legally acceptable alternative identity checks.

For example, if a villager cannot receive an OTP because of network failure, a government service should follow its approved alternative process rather than assume that the villager's identity is false. Similarly, a person with limited literacy may need assistance to complete an application while retaining appropriate control over their personal information.

The purpose of digital public infrastructure is to make useful services more accessible and reliable. Merely replacing a physical queue with an inaccessible online procedure does not necessarily improve inclusion.

Prelims focus

  • Governance determines responsibilities, participation rules, accountability and safeguards.
  • Open standards can support interoperability and reduce vendor lock-in.
  • Open-source software can still require substantial maintenance and operating expenditure.
  • Technical, financial, institutional, social and environmental sustainability are distinct considerations.
  • Assisted access and lawful alternatives help reduce digital exclusion.
  • Trap: Open-source status alone does not guarantee security, inclusion or sustainability.

[Sources: G20, Framework for Systems of Digital Public Infrastructure, 19 August 2023, principles for secure, interoperable and inclusive systems; Digital Public Goods Alliance, 'Digital Public Goods Standard,' privacy, documentation and standards indicators; NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class 11, Chapter 8, 'Infrastructure,' printed pp. 140–143; NCERT, Social and Political Life III, Class 8, Chapter 9, 'Public Facilities,' printed pp. 112–117; sources consulted 5 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Six connected dimensions sustain digital public infrastructure: technical, financial, institutional, social, environmental and governance.
pictures.caption: Successful digital public infrastructure depends on technology, governance, inclusion and continuing maintenance.

title: Governance, Inclusion and Long-Term Sustainability of Digital Public Infrastructure

body:
Digital public services in Gujarat

Gujarat provides practical examples of how digital identity, common login systems, document verification and departmental integration can support public administration. The State's initiatives also illustrate why a digital service needs more than an online website: citizens must be able to complete applications, provide suitable documents and receive the approved service.

Digital Gujarat Portal

The Digital Gujarat Portal is a common service platform developed to provide access to various Government of Gujarat services through a single online entry point. Gujarat Informatics Limited identifies the portal's objectives as improving the accessibility, efficiency and transparency of citizen-facing services.

The platform supports features such as citizen registration, service applications, document submission and access through multiple service channels. The availability of a service, the required supporting documents and the accepted authentication method depend on the relevant department and application.

Gujarat Citizen Single Sign-On

Gujarat Citizen Single Sign On, also described as GOG eSuvidha or Gujarat SSO, provides a unified login arrangement for participating government services.

According to Gujarat Informatics Limited, the initiative uses a central citizen profile and supports verification through relevant identity-document information, including Aadhaar, PAN, ration-card or Child Tracking ID details where applicable. Its objective is to reduce repeated registration and provide a consistent identity profile for connected services.

Gujarat SSO is an example of an integrated authentication service. It does not mean that every government department must expose all its records to every other department. Each service must still apply its own permissions and requirements.

Digital Seva Setu: digital access at village level

Digital Seva Setu was launched in Gujarat on 8 October 2020. It aims to provide citizen services at the village level through e-Gram centres, reducing the need to travel to taluka or district offices for services available through the initiative.

Digital Seva Setu connects administrative workflows across participating departments. Depending on the particular service, applications and supporting documents can be submitted through e-Gram, checked by the appropriate officials and processed through integrated electronic systems. Service outputs may be provided digitally, through DigiLocker where supported, or in physical form.

The use of an e-Gram centre is significant for inclusion. A person who does not own a smartphone or who needs help completing an application may still access a service through an assisted channel. The staff member's assistance does not remove the need for proper identity checks or responsible handling of personal information.

How the concepts operate together

Consider a villager applying for an income certificate through an available government service channel. The applicant supplies the required information and supporting documents. The system identifies the applicant's record and uses an accepted authentication or verification method where necessary. An authorised official checks the application's conditions and issues the certificate if they are satisfied.

If the service is integrated with an approved digital document system, a digitally issued certificate may become available for later permitted use. If the applicant has difficulty with internet access or a particular authentication method, assistance and applicable alternative procedures can help avoid unnecessary exclusion.

Notice the separate roles: the identifier refers to the applicant, authentication checks the claimant, authorization determines access, interoperability supports permitted information exchange, and the government department remains responsible for the administrative decision.

Complete comparison for objective examinations

TermCentral questionDistinguishing fact
Digital identityWho is represented in the system?Attributes and identifiers describe an individual.
AuthenticationIs the claimant legitimate?Uses approved evidence such as PIN, OTP or biometrics.
AuthorizationWhat may the claimant do?Checks permissions after authentication.
FederationWho confirms identity for another service?An identity provider supplies trusted authentication information.
Open standardHow can systems work compatibly?Publicly accessible agreed specification.
Open-source softwareCan the code be reused and modified?Rights arise from the applicable open-source licence.
Open dataCan suitable data be accessed and reused?Publication and reuse are governed by licence and exclusions.
Digital public goodIs the solution openly reusable for public benefit?Must satisfy applicable DPG criteria for formal recognition.
Digital public infrastructureWhich shared digital functions support many services?Identity, payments and trusted data exchange are key examples.

One-glance conceptual summary

The central relationship is that digital identity helps establish and verify the person, authentication confirms the claimant, authorization regulates access, and interoperability allows suitably governed systems to work together. Open technologies can make components easier to reuse and connect. Digital public goods can supply reusable solutions, while digital public infrastructure provides shared capabilities used by multiple services. Privacy, inclusion, governance and sustainability determine whether those capabilities deliver lasting public value.

Prelims focus

  • Digital Gujarat provides a common access point for Government of Gujarat services.
  • Gujarat SSO, or GOG eSuvidha, supports unified access to participating services.
  • Digital Seva Setu was launched on 8 October 2020.
  • Digital Seva Setu delivers participating services through village-level e-Gram centres.
  • Aadhaar, UPI and DigiLocker primarily address identity, payments and digital documents, respectively.
  • Trap: Digitising an application process does not eliminate departmental eligibility checks, privacy obligations or the need for accessible service channels.

[Sources: Gujarat Informatics Limited, 'Digital Gujarat Portal (Common Service Portal),' project description and features; Gujarat Informatics Limited, 'Gujarat Citizen Single Sign On (GOG eSuvidha),' project description; Gujarat Informatics Limited, 'Digital Seva Setu,' objective, process and launch date, 8 October 2020; Gujarat Department of Science and Technology, 'Projects and Initiatives,' Digital Gujarat and Digital Seva Setu; G20, Framework for Systems of Digital Public Infrastructure, 19 August 2023; sources consulted 5 November 2026.]
